name: Tapinarof

lead: Tapinarof (Vtama) is a prescription cream that clears the visible red, scaly plaques of psoriasis and eczema, so skin looks clearer and smoother. It is steroid-free and approved in the US for plaque psoriasis in adults and atopic dermatitis in adults and children aged 2 and older.

It activates the aryl hydrocarbon receptor in skin cells, which lab studies link to less inflammation and better barrier proteins; the label says the exact mechanism is unknown. Two phase 3 trials in plaque psoriasis were published in 2021, and a phase 2b trial reported efficacy in atopic dermatitis. Seborrheic dermatitis is described as under study, with no trial found in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is a 1% cream applied to affected patches as directed by a prescriber, as an ongoing treatment for the skin condition rather than a cosmetic. People use it where plaques show, and results build over weeks of regular use.
Label-listed reactions in psoriasis include folliculitis, nasopharyngitis, contact dermatitis and headache. Human pregnancy data are insufficient. It is prescription only.

angle.text: Tapinarof clears the visible plaques and redness of psoriasis and eczema, leaving skin clearer and smoother. It works by activating the AhR receptor in skin cells, which lowers inflammation. Phase 3 trials support its psoriasis use.

lead: Tapinarof (brand name Vtama) is a 1% topical cream and an aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) agonist. The US FDA label lists it for plaque psoriasis in adults and atopic dermatitis in adults and children aged 2 and older.[1] For appearance, it targets visible skin disease: the red, scaly plaques of psoriasis and the red, dry, itchy patches of eczema, including on exposed areas such as the head and neck, where it has been studied specifically.[1][2]

It is steroid-free, which makes it part of a group of newer nonsteroidal creams used when people want to treat visible patches without topical corticosteroids.[3][4] The compound is a stilbenoid produced by Photorhabdus bacteria that live symbiotically with Heterorhabditis nematodes.[5]

Its mechanism in these conditions is described on the label as unknown, although laboratory work shows it binds and activates AhR in skin cells, with effects on interleukin-17 and the barrier proteins filaggrin and loricrin.[1][6][7] Two phase 3 trials in plaque psoriasis were published in 2021,[7] pivotal ADORING trials in atopic dermatitis followed,[8] and a phase 2b trial had earlier reported efficacy in adolescents and adults.[9] Seborrheic dermatitis is described as under study, but no trial for it has been published.

paras: Per the US label, Vtama is indicated for plaque psoriasis in adults and for atopic dermatitis in adults and pediatric patients 2 years and older.[1] Grokipedia reports FDA approval for psoriasis in May 2022 and for atopic dermatitis in December 2024.[10]

Tapinarof is a naturally derived compound that binds and activates AhR, and its anti-inflammatory properties in mice and human skin were shown to depend on that activation.[6] Reviews describe AhR activity as strengthening skin barrier function and increasing filaggrin expression.[11]

The phase 3 psoriasis report states that tapinarof modulates interleukin-17 expression and the skin-barrier proteins filaggrin and loricrin.[7] In atopic dermatitis, the ADORING publication describes downregulation of pro-inflammatory Th2 cytokines, upregulation of skin-barrier components and reduced oxidative stress.[8] Wikipedia describes it as a first-in-class medication.[5]

Tapinarof is a small stilbenoid, 3,5-dihydroxy-4-isopropylstilbene, with the formula C17H18O2 and a molar mass of about 254 g/mol; its other names are benvitimod and the development code GSK-2894512, and tapinarof is the WHO International Nonproprietary Name listed in 2017.[5] In nature it is made by Photorhabdus bacteria, such as Photorhabdus luminescens living with Heterorhabditis nematodes, which infect insect larvae. Wikipedia reports that experiments in wax moth larvae suggest it has antibiotic properties that limit competing microbes and prevent the infected carcass from putrefying.[5]

Tapinarof is regulated as a prescription-only medicine. Wikipedia notes that when the FDA approved it in May 2022, the company described it as the first topical novel chemical entity launched for psoriasis in the US in 25 years, and that the FDA considers it a first-in-class medication; Health Canada lists it as prescription-only under the name Nduvra.[5]

For people whose psoriasis or eczema shows on the face, scalp, neck or hands, topical options that avoid corticosteroids are of practical interest because long-term steroid use on thin facial skin is associated with skin thinning. Reviews of newer nonsteroidal topicals list tapinarof alongside roflumilast, and a dedicated registered study examines it in head and neck psoriasis.[3][4][2] The published literature does not compare tapinarof directly with other nonsteroidal creams.

Tapinarof (also called benvitimod, with the development code GSK-2894512) originates from the bacterial stilbenoid produced by Photorhabdus bacteria, and its AhR-mediated anti-inflammatory activity in mice and humans was reported in 2017.[6][5] The FDA approved it for plaque psoriasis in May 2022 as a first-in-class medication, and Grokipedia reports atopic dermatitis approval in December 2024; the label is held by Organon.[1][10][5] Reviews now list it with roflumilast among newer nonsteroidal topical options, and the American Academy of Dermatology 2025 focused update on adult atopic dermatitis addresses newly approved topical therapies.[3][12][4]

Two identical phase 3 vehicle-controlled trials in plaque psoriasis (NCT03956355, n=510; NCT03983980, n=515) enrolled adults with baseline Physician Global Assessment scores of 2 (mild) to 4 (severe) and were published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2021.[7][13][14] Wikipedia reports that the 1% cream used once daily was superior to vehicle in reducing psoriasis severity over 12 weeks.[5] A long-term extension of 763 adults is registered,[15] a treat-to-target analysis of the phase 3 data has been published,[16] and two Japanese phase 3 psoriasis trials have been reported.[17]

In atopic dermatitis, a phase 2 dose-finding study and a phase 2b trial in adolescents and adults came first.[9][18] Two 8-week phase 3 ADORING trials randomized 813 adults and children down to 2 years of age to tapinarof or vehicle once daily,[8] and ADORING 3 is a 48-week open-label extension examining skin clearance and treatment-free intervals.[19][20] Two Japanese phase 3 atopic dermatitis trials were also published.[21]

Registered studies include a pediatric maximal-use study (n=36), a head-and-neck psoriasis study (n=31), a study in psoriasis patients on biologics (n=30), and small studies in cutaneous lupus and palmoplantar keratoderma.[22][23][24][2]

In plaque psoriasis the most common adverse reactions on the label (incidence of 1 percent or more) were folliculitis, nasopharyngitis, contact dermatitis, headache, pruritus and influenza. In atopic dermatitis they included upper respiratory tract infection, folliculitis, lower respiratory tract infection, headache, asthma, vomiting, ear infection, pain in extremity and abdominal pain.[1]

Human pregnancy data are insufficient to assess risk of major birth defects or miscarriage; in animal reproduction studies, subcutaneous tapinarof in pregnant rats and rabbits produced no significant adverse effects at multiples of the maximum recommended human dose.[1]
